column2: The sky looks blue because sunlight is made of many colors, and air molecules scatter short blue waves much more than long red ones. That scattered blue light comes at us from every direction, so the whole sky glows blue.
At sunset, sunlight travels through much more air to reach you. Most of the blue light gets scattered away on the long trip, so the light that is left looks orange and red.

A rainbow forms when sunlight shines into raindrops. Each drop bends the light, bounces it off the back of the drop and bends it again, which splits white light into its colors. You see a rainbow when the sun is behind you and rain is in front of you.

We have seasons because Earth's axis is tilted about 23 degrees. For part of the year your half of Earth leans toward the sun and gets more direct sunlight and longer days, which is summer. Half a year later it leans away, which is winter.

Photosynthesis is how plants make their own food. Their leaves take in sunlight, water and carbon dioxide from the air, and use the light's energy to turn them into sugar. Oxygen is released as a by-product, which is the oxygen we breathe.

The moon has phases because we see different amounts of its sunlit side as it orbits Earth. When it is between Earth and the sun we see a new moon, and when Earth is between them we see a full moon. The whole cycle takes about 29.5 days.

Tides are caused mostly by the moon's gravity pulling on Earth's oceans. The water bulges toward the moon and also on the opposite side of Earth, so most coasts get two high tides and two low tides each day.

Lightning is a giant spark of electricity between clouds, or between a cloud and the ground. It heats the air so fast that the air explodes outward, and that shock wave is the thunder you hear. Light travels faster than sound, so you see the flash first.

Gravity is the pull that every object with mass has on every other object. Earth is so massive that its pull keeps us on the ground and keeps the moon in orbit. The more mass something has and the closer you are to it, the stronger the pull.

A volcano is an opening in Earth's crust where melted rock called magma rises from deep below. Pressure from gas and magma builds up until it bursts out as lava, ash and gas. Many volcanoes sit where the plates of Earth's crust meet.

Earthquakes happen when huge slabs of Earth's crust, called plates, suddenly slip past each other. Stress builds up along a fault until the rock breaks or slides, and the released energy travels through the ground as shaking waves.

Clouds form when warm, moist air rises and cools. Cooler air can't hold as much water vapor, so the vapor condenses into tiny droplets or ice crystals around specks of dust. When the droplets grow heavy enough, they fall as rain or snow.

Snow forms when water vapor in very cold clouds freezes straight into ice crystals. The crystals grow six-sided branches as more vapor freezes on them, and they stick together into snowflakes that are heavy enough to fall.

Wind is air moving from places of high pressure to places of low pressure. The sun heats Earth unevenly, so some air warms, rises and leaves lower pressure behind, and cooler air rushes in to fill the gap.

In the water cycle, the sun warms oceans and lakes so water evaporates into the air. The vapor rises, cools and condenses into clouds, then falls as rain or snow. The water flows back into rivers and seas, and the cycle starts again.

Your heart is a muscle that pumps blood around your body. Blood picks up oxygen in the lungs, the heart pushes it out through arteries to every cell, and veins bring it back. An adult heart beats about 60 to 100 times a minute.
When you breathe in, your lungs fill with air. Tiny air sacs pass oxygen into your blood and take carbon dioxide out of it. When you breathe out, the carbon dioxide leaves your body.

Sleep gives your brain and body time to rest and repair. While you sleep, your brain sorts memories and clears out waste. Dreams happen mostly during REM sleep, when the brain is very active even though the body is still.

A vaccine trains your immune system to recognize a germ before you meet the real thing. It contains a harmless piece or weakened form of the germ, so your body makes antibodies and memory cells that can fight the actual infection quickly.
A fever is your body raising its temperature to fight an infection. Many germs grow poorly when it is warmer, and the heat helps your immune cells work faster.

Digestion breaks food into tiny pieces your body can use. Chewing starts it, the stomach mixes food with acid, and the small intestine absorbs the nutrients into your blood. What is left moves to the large intestine, where water is taken back.

A magnet has a magnetic field because tiny regions inside it, where the electrons spin the same way, all line up. Every magnet has a north and a south pole. Opposite poles attract and matching poles push each other away.

Electricity is the flow of tiny charged particles called electrons. When a wire connects a battery's two ends, electrons move through the wire as a current, and that moving energy can light a bulb or run a motor.
A battery stores energy in chemicals. When you connect it to a circuit, a chemical reaction inside pushes electrons out of one end, through the device and back into the other end.

The internet is a huge network of computers connected by cables, fiber and radio. Information is cut into small packets that travel separately through many routers and are put back together when they arrive.

A computer follows instructions very quickly. Its processor does simple math and logic steps billions of times a second, memory holds the data it is working on, and storage keeps files when the power is off.

An airplane flies because its wings are shaped and angled so that air moves faster over the top and is pushed down underneath. That creates lift, an upward force. The engines provide thrust to keep the plane moving fast enough for the wings to work.
Things float when they push aside, or displace, a weight of water equal to their own weight. A steel ship is hollow, so it displaces a lot of water for its weight, and the water pushes it up.
Stars shine because of nuclear fusion in their cores. Enormous pressure and heat squeeze hydrogen atoms together into helium, and that releases huge amounts of energy as light and heat.
The sun is a star, a giant ball of hot gas about 150 million kilometers away. Fusion in its core turns hydrogen into helium and gives off the light and heat that make life on Earth possible.

A black hole is a place where gravity is so strong that nothing, not even light, can escape. Many form when a very large star runs out of fuel and its core collapses into a tiny, extremely dense point.

A solar eclipse happens when the moon passes between the sun and Earth and blocks the sun's light. A lunar eclipse happens when Earth passes between the sun and the moon, and Earth's shadow falls on the moon.

Most dinosaurs died out about 66 million years ago. The best-supported explanation is that a huge asteroid hit Earth near Mexico, throwing up dust that blocked sunlight and changed the climate, while large volcanic eruptions added to the damage.

Evolution is the way living things change over many generations. Individuals with traits that help them survive and have young pass those traits on more often, so over long periods populations adapt and new species can form.
DNA is the instruction manual inside your cells. It is a long twisted molecule whose sequence of four chemical letters spells out genes, which tell the cell how to build proteins.

Bees make honey from flower nectar. They sip the nectar, store it in a special stomach, and pass it to other bees in the hive, who add enzymes and fan it with their wings until most of the water evaporates and it thickens into honey.

Leaves change color in autumn because trees stop making chlorophyll, the green pigment, as days get shorter. When the green fades, yellow and orange pigments that were there all along show through, and some trees make new red pigments.
Ice floats because water expands when it freezes. Its molecules lock into an open pattern, so ice is less dense than liquid water and sits on top.

The ocean is salty because rivers carry tiny amounts of dissolved minerals from rocks into the sea. When seawater evaporates, the water leaves but the salt stays, so salt has built up over millions of years.
Soap cleans because its molecules have two ends: one end sticks to water and the other sticks to oil and grease. The soap surrounds the grease and lets the water carry it away.
A microwave oven makes tiny waves that make water molecules in food spin back and forth very fast. That motion creates heat, which cooks the food from the inside and outside at the same time.

The greenhouse effect is how gases like carbon dioxide trap heat in the atmosphere. Sunlight warms Earth, and the planet gives off heat, but these gases absorb some of it and keep it near the surface. Adding more of them makes the planet warmer.
Recycling turns used materials such as paper, glass, metal and some plastics into new products. It saves raw materials and energy and keeps waste out of landfills.
Inflation means prices rise over time, so the same amount of money buys less. It often happens when there is more money chasing the same amount of goods, or when making things gets more expensive.
Nobody is completely sure why we yawn. Scientists think it may help cool the brain or help us stay alert when we are tired or bored, and it is famously contagious.
Hiccups happen when your diaphragm, the muscle under your lungs, suddenly twitches. That makes you suck in air, and your vocal cords snap shut, which makes the hic sound.
